newsitem.title: INDIA: BONDS POINT TO INDIA RATE CUT, COST OF FUNDS DO NOT.
newsitem.headline: BONDS POINT TO INDIA RATE CUT, COST OF FUNDS DO NOT.

text.p: Indian banks' surplus liquidity has pushed down yields on bonds, leading to expectations of a fall in lending rates but deposit rates will have to fall further first, bankers said.
"At the moment, I do not see any scope for a further cut in lending rates," said the credit head of a public sector bank. "Our cost of funds is still pretty much the same."
They said although bond yields have fallen by around 200 basis points since the beginning of the financial year on April 1, bank lending rates are unlikely to be cut in the near future.
Bankers said the fall in bond yields did not necessarily indicate that general interest rates should come down.

"With demand for credit at a low level, banks are pumping money into bonds, driving prices up," a foreign banker said. "This may not last long if credit demand picks up as most people expect it to in the second half of the year."
Bank deposits grew by 765.61 billion rupees in the last year to touch 5,246.94 billion on July 25. But loans grew only 276.67 billion rupees to 2,785.34 billion.
Banks have lowered deposit and lending rates several times in the last year in response to central bank reductions in cash reserve ratio requirements and in the bank rate.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) cut cash reserve ratio requirements for banks to 10 percent from 12 percent between October 1996 and January 1997.

The RBI has twice cut its bank rate, the rate at which banks borrow from the central bank, this fiscal year (1997/98, April-March) to lower the rate to 10 percent from 12 percent at the beginning of April.
Leading state-run banks charge a prime lending rate of 13.5 percent per annum against 16 percent last year.
Deposit rates have also come down by 200-300 basis points, with banks giving a maximum of only 8.0 percent per annum for deposits with maturities up to one year against 11.0 percent last year.
"True, we have cut both deposit and lending rates. But the effect on deposits will be felt only later this year," the public sector bank's credit head said.
When banks cut interest rates, the revised rates take immediate effect on all loans but the lower deposit rates only apply to fresh deposits.
"Our older deposits are still locked in at higher rates," the banker said. "Our cost of funds has not come down much."
Bankers said interest rates had also come down mainly for shorter-maturity deposits.
"The fall (in interest rates) has been more pronounced for deposits with maturity up to one year," said another public sector banker. "Longer-term deposits have not been affected much."
"But short-term deposits comprise only a small part of our total deposits," he said.
